summary: This extension to SIP event notification lets a subscriber subscribe to an entire homogeneous list of resources instead of sending a SUBSCRIBE for each one. The subscriber is then notified when the state of any resource in the list changes.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking each friend one by one whether they're online, you ask once about your whole friends list and get told whenever one changes.

questions: subscribe to a list in sip
what is a sip resource list server
how do i subscribe to a list in sip
subtitle: Subscribe once to a whole list of things, such as a buddy list, and get told whenever any of them changes.

tldr.problem: A SIP subscriber who cares about many resources would have to send a SUBSCRIBE and refreshes for each one, which is costly where bandwidth is limited.
tldr.mechanism: The subscriber sends one SUBSCRIBE to a list URI. A resource list server (RLS) watches the members and sends NOTIFY requests carrying a multipart/related body: an XML meta-information document plus the state of each resource.
tldr.outcome: One subscription replaces many, the RLS can batch and rate-limit notifications, and lists can be nested. The price is new complexity around state merging and authorization.

today: RFC 4662 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2006. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with One Subscription per Resource
sections.content:
SIP event notification lets a subscriber send a SUBSCRIBE request for a resource and receive NOTIFY requests when its state changes. If someone cares about a whole list of resources, they would need a SUBSCRIBE for each one. The RFC lists the costs: many initial SUBSCRIBE requests and refreshes, notifiers that may insist on short refresh intervals, and NOTIFY traffic at a higher volume than the subscriber wants. This matters most on bandwidth-limited networks such as wireless ones.

RFC 4662 extends RFC 3265 so that a resource list, identified by a URI, stands for zero or more other URIs. The notifier for the list is called a resource list server (RLS). The list and its members do not have to be in the subscriber's domain or in each other's.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking about each friend separately means lots of messages. Asking once about a whole list means far fewer.

sections.title: Lists, Virtual and Back-End Subscriptions
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few terms. A list subscription is a subscription to a resource list, where the RLS acts as notifier. For each resource in the list the RLS keeps a virtual subscription, a logical construct. When the RLS is not the authority for a resource, the virtual subscription is tied to a back-end subscription, where the RLS acts as a subscriber (SIP or otherwise) to learn the state.

A list subscription must be homogeneous: one event package applies to every resource in the list. Lists can nest, so subscribing to a list may produce a tree of virtual subscriptions whose leaves use the event type named in the Event header. How the list is created and maintained is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper keeps a pretend subscription for every friend on your list, and checks with other helpers for the friends it does not know about itself.

sections.title: Negotiating Support
sections.content:
Support is signalled with the option tag eventlist. A client willing to handle lists includes it in a Supported header field in SUBSCRIBE requests. If the target URI is a list, the RLS puts Require: eventlist in its response to the SUBSCRIBE and in every NOTIFY in that subscription. Putting eventlist in a Require header of a SUBSCRIBE is NOT RECOMMENDED, and implementations SHOULD NOT send Supported: eventlist in anything except SUBSCRIBE.

Nothing in a SIP URI shows whether it is a list. So a request to a list URI without eventlist support will typically get a 421 (Extension Required) response, even though RFC 3261 normally advises avoiding 421.

Compliant implementations MUST support multipart/related and application/rlmi+xml, and MUST list them in the Accept header of a SUBSCRIBE. A long subscription duration is RECOMMENDED, since the point is to reduce message volume; the default comes from the event package.
sections.plainLanguage: When you knock, you say 'I understand list answers'. If you do not and the door leads to a list, the helper tells you that you need to learn that first.

sections.title: Notification Bodies and the RLMI Document
sections.content:
List notifications carry a multipart/related body. The root part MUST be a Resource List Meta-Information (RLMI) document of type application/rlmi+xml. The remaining parts hold the actual state of each resource, in the content type of the underlying event package.

The <list> element has three mandatory attributes. uri is the list URI. version is a number from 0 to 2^32-1, which MUST be 0 in the first NOTIFY and increase by exactly one with each later NOTIFY. fullState says whether the document covers every resource in the list; the first NOTIFY, and the first after a SUBSCRIBE refresh, MUST carry full state. An optional cid points to a part with aggregate state.

Inside it, each <resource> has a mandatory uri and optional human-readable <name> elements (with xml:lang). Each <instance> inside a resource represents one notifier; several can exist when the event package allows forking. An instance has an opaque id, a state of active, pending or terminated, a reason that MUST be present when terminated, and a cid that MUST be present when active and names the part holding the state. A cid may refer only to top-level parts of the multipart body in which its RLMI document is the root.

A subscription is either a single-resource one or a list one for its whole life. An RLS MUST NOT mix NOTIFY messages with and without RLMI in one subscription.
sections.plainLanguage: The first page of each reply is a table of contents saying who is on the list and which later page holds each friend's news.

sections.title: Generating and Merging Notifications
sections.content:
How and when the RLS sends NOTIFY requests is left to the implementer. A baseline is to send one whenever any resource changes, but an RLS may buffer changes and send them in batches, which gives rate limiting on behalf of the subscriber. If a resource's state is not yet known, its <resource> appears with no <instance>. Terminated instances SHOULD appear in the first NOTIFY after they go away.

The subscriber keeps a table with one row per resource URI. For a full state notification, it first checks that the version is greater than its local one, discarding the document otherwise, then flushes the table and refills it from the document.

For a partial state notification there are three cases. A version exactly one higher than local is processed normally. A version more than one higher means a NOTIFY was lost: the local version is set to the new value, the document is processed, and the subscriber SHOULD send a refresh to trigger a full state notification. A version less than or equal to the local one is discarded. Each listed resource is then added or updated, and rows that become terminated MAY be removed.

Forking makes little sense for list subscriptions, so a subscriber MUST NOT install multiple subscriptions when the initial request forks.
sections.plainLanguage: Each reply has a number. If you see number 5 then 6, fine. If you jump from 5 to 8, you know you missed some, so you ask for a full update.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content: The RFC walks through a presence subscription to a nested list, sip:adam-buddies@pres.vancouver.example.com, by a subscriber at sip:adam@vancouver.example.com. The terminal sends a SUBSCRIBE with Event: presence, Supported: eventlist and Accept headers for the PIDF, RLMI and multipart types. The RLS answers 200 OK with Require: eventlist and immediately sends a NOTIFY with full state, covering the presence it already knows locally. For other entries it subscribes to servers in other domains, and each reply triggers further NOTIFY requests to the terminal. The example is non-normative.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask the local helper about your buddy list. It tells you what it knows right away, then asks other helpers and passes along their news as it arrives.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When an RLS uses back-end subscriptions, the end user is no longer the direct subscriber, so direct authentication is lost. If the subscriber and RLS share a domain, the RLS can authenticate the subscriber and add an Identity header to back-end subscriptions, acting as the authentication service defined in RFC 4474. An RLS using SIP back-end subscriptions MUST be able to act as an authentication service, if local policy allows. Across domains this does not work, so such an RLS SHOULD subscribe under its own identity, normally obtaining only public information. A subscriber MAY subscribe directly to the listed resources and SHOULD prefer that data.

An RLS MUST NOT present the result of one back-end subscription to more than one user unless it has the full authorization policy and has determined it is not violated. Even then this is NOT RECOMMENDED.

MIME bodies may be signed or encrypted, so an RLS should not modify them, and SHOULD pass along support for multipart/signed and application/pkcs7-mime. Because lists can nest and may contain themselves, an RLS that creates back-end subscriptions MUST implement safeguards against infinite loops.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper must not show you a secret just because it already told someone else. And it must not get stuck forever following a list that points back to itself.
